So ought it be? There is a problem with privatizing many things. The private economy is obsessed with money. And this can get in the way of performance or value. For instance how much would you be willing to pay or even go into debt for life saving health care? Dead men don't have much use for money. The argument we use in the US to justify this is the invisible hand of the market. If company A is gouging you then company B will start up and earn lots of money by charging a more fair price. But the reality is that companies stand to earn much more refusing to compete between themselves, or at the minimum minimizing competition. And for most modern fields there are extreme barriers to entry, the least of which not being economic. As we advance technologically these barriers will only grow.

Consequently we've now seen most developed nations begin to nationalize many critical services, such as health care and education. In fact the United States is the only major developed nation with no real sort of universal health care, and no - being legally forced to pay money to private middle men does not amount to universal health care. And now the United States pays far more than any other country for healthcare, and it's rapidly increasing. Here is a graph. The natural retort should be, "Well yeah. We pay more. But you get what you pay for!" Oft touted anecdotes of people being refused or having to wait weeks for treatment in countries with universal healthcare notwithstanding, the United States actually has some of the worst health outcomes in the developed world to show for paying far more than any other country. The private system simply doesn't work well for things that are seen to have a practically limitless value for people. Education is another thing along these lines and you can find similar data for that as well.

So back to the topic of the internet, I do believe it also qualifies as one of these things that has a limitless value for people. The vast majority of communication is already done on the internet and I'd assume entertainment, self learning, remote work, and much more. This is something that absolutely ought to be a fundamental right because it's too open to exploitation in the private market. And consequently the US, like many other things along these lines, now pays more than most any other developed country for some of the lowest quality internet access. Our state of internet (and economics) is just embarrassing when a country like South Korea, which was a veritable third world country in the 60s, is now offering 200 Mbit connections for no contract, no fees, and less than $30 a month.

Wow, you weren't kidding about how unhelpful most definitions are. Every article/explanation I've run across is 90% busy words and 10% vague attachment to moderism.

This was the most helpful explanation I found.

  1. premodernism: Original meaning is possessed by authority (for example, the Catholic Church). The individual is dominated by tradition.
  2. modernism: The enlightenment-humanist rejection of tradition and authority in favour of reason and natural science. This is founded upon the assumption of the autonomous individual as the sole source of meaning and truth--the Cartesian cogito. Progress and novelty are valorized within a linear conception of history--a history of a "real" world that becomes increasingly real or objectified. One could view this as a Protestant mode of consciousness.
  3. postmodernism: A rejection of the sovereign autonomous individual with an emphasis upon anarchic collective, anonymous experience. Collage, diversity, the mystically unrepresentable, Dionysian passion are the foci of attention. Most importantly we see the dissolution of distinctions, the merging of subject and object, self and other. This is a sarcastic playful parody of western modernity and the "John Wayne" individual and a radical, anarchist rejection of all attempts to define, reify or re-present the human subject.

As far as, post-postmoderism and Metamoderism goes; I think it's just a continuation of the questioning of postmodernism, which is the questioning of moderism, which is the questioning of pre-moderism, which is the questioning of ..., which is the questioning of ..., etc.

So it's the endless debate of how reality is perceived/measured and questioning the previous theories that seem too simplistic and have negative effects on society as a whole.

Best ELI5 I can think of. Moderism opened the doors to questioning our traditions, by witnessing the effects different traditions have had on other communities. In turn, every expansion of that Moderism view point, is trying to constantly challenge past theories so we never get locked into more unquestioned traditions that can slow social progress.
